analysis.one_liner: Imposes new requirements on pharmacy benefit managers in Medicare and employer health plans.
analysis.headline: Introduced September 14, 2026 and sent to three House committees, the bill has sat without a hearing or vote, with four cosponsors split evenly between the parties.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers are the middlemen that employers and Medicare hire to manage drug benefits. They negotiate with drugmakers, decide which drugs are covered and what patients pay at the counter, and take a share of the money flowing through the system. This bill would write new federal rules for how they operate in Medicare and in employer plans covered by the federal employee-benefits law, aimed at reining in their pricing practices.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients filling prescriptions under Medicare and through employer plans, who could pay less at the pharmacy counter and see more of the savings from drug price negotiations passed through instead of retained by the middleman. Independent pharmacies also benefit if the bill curbs the reimbursement practices that squeeze them, since they get paid largely by the same companies.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds requirements for pharmacy benefit managers under both Medicare (title XVIII of the Social Security Act) and the federal law governing employer health plans, extending scrutiny to the two largest channels through which Americans get prescription drugs.
It was introduced with cosponsors from both parties, 2 Democrats and 2 Republicans, which is notable in an area where bipartisan agreement on drug middleman reform is common.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers — the large ones are owned by or affiliated with the biggest insurers and pharmacy chains — would bear the cost of complying with new rules and could lose revenue if they can no longer keep part of drug price savings. Some compliance costs could ultimately flow to insurers, employers, and premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their parent companies

drawbacks.text: Pharmacy benefit managers argue their negotiated rebates from drugmakers help lower insurance premiums, so curbing their pricing practices could push some of the cost back onto premiums and employer plans rather than lowering net prices.

New federal requirements layered onto employer plans governed by the employee-benefits law can raise administrative costs for employers who sponsor coverage, and the bill's requirements are untested — how much actually reaches the pharmacy counter depends on rules that would follow.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is real and large: prescription drug costs are a top expense for older Americans and working families, and the middleman system is widely criticized for capturing savings at patients' expense. But the bill is early-stage and its actual strength depends on the requirements' details, which are not spelled out in the title; a weak version could add paperwork without moving prices much.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to three House committees, but in the closing weeks of the session none of them has taken it up.

narrative.text: Representative Ryan Mackenzie of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on September 14, 2026.
The same day, it was referred to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce — with consideration to be divided as the Speaker determines.
Four members cosponsored: 2 Democrats and 2 Republicans.
No committee markup, hearing, or floor action has been recorded since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The pharmacy benefit manager industry, which collects fees and spread on hundreds of billions of dollars in drug spending each year, is better off while the bill sits without committee action; patients hoping for lower drug costs are no worse off but no better off.

for.name: Rep. Ryan Mackenzie
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to three committees with jurisdiction over health, Medicare, and employee benefits.

for.name: Four House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original supporters, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Pharmacy benefit manager industry
against.role: Major PBMs (owned by or affiliated with large insurers and pharmacy chains)
against.what_they_did: The industry has a long record of lobbying against federal restrictions on PBM pricing and transparency, and no committee has advanced the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship is evenly split, with 2 Democratic and 2 Republican cosponsors joining a Republican sponsor.

industries.note: PBMs are paid to manage drug benefits and profit by keeping a share of negotiated prices and by setting pharmacy reimbursement; new federal requirements in Medicare and employer plans threaten that revenue. Their interest runs against patients who pay the resulting higher prices at the counter.

Small pharmacies are reimbursed largely by PBM-owned pharmacy managers and have pushed for reform; requirements on PBMs could ease the reimbursement squeeze that has driven independent pharmacies to close.

industries.industry: Insurers and employers sponsoring drug coverage
industries.note: Employers would face new compliance requirements on plans they sponsor, but they also bear the cost of drug benefits, so stronger PBM rules could lower what they pay for coverage.

analysis.trajectory: Referred simultaneously to three committees in mid-September, with the session ending in early January, the bill is unlikely to see a hearing, markup, or floor vote; first-term bills with a handful of cosponsors rarely advance this late in a Congress.
